caseStudies.title: Garmin health coach
caseStudies.summary: From never coding to an AI coach that plans my marathon training.

starr.situation: I was **a product manager who had never coded**. I wanted a fitness coach that knew my Garmin data and could help plan my training.
starr.task: I set out to prove I could build it with low-code tools.
starr.action: Strava's API was paid-only, so I used **an open-source Garmin Connect pipeline from GitHub**. **I built n8n flows** that exported my data to CSV, **then a Python script** that sent it straight to a spreadsheet. The hardest part was merging data points from several files into one source a Gemini chatbot could use.
starr.result: It worked, but it was not sustainable. n8n in Docker only ran while my laptop was on, and Gemini's free tier often failed to respond. **I rebuilt it in Claude**, which now plans my marathon training.
starr.reflection: Building it **sharpened how I judge developer effort**. I now challenge estimates, see where real complexity sits, and find faster ways to test ideas.

caseStudies.title: Finance dashboard
caseStudies.summary: Seven payment methods in one view, reviewed daily in under a minute.

starr.situation: During my move to Kuala Lumpur, I manage a fixed budget across **seven payment methods**. No app showed them in one place.
starr.task: I set out to build my own expense dashboard, solo, **with Claude Code**.
starr.action: I built it in **Next.js and TypeScript, with Supabase**. Revolut and ING **sync through open banking**. My credit card, Wise, ShopeePay, Grab and Touch 'n Go only offer statements, which I first uploaded by hand. To automate that cheaply, **I added the Anthropic API** for a few euros a month. A daily job now reads saved screenshots into a review list.
starr.result: **I use it every day.** Reviewing yesterday's transactions takes under a minute, and I see my spending across budget pools.
starr.reflection: I am investor, customer, developer and product manager in one. I enjoy building, so nice-to-haves tempt me. **I now guard priorities** and give the user, me, time to adopt before adding more.

caseStudies.title: Job hunting platform
caseStudies.summary: Claude Code sub-agents that research roles and track my applications.

caseStudies.title: AI sales agent
caseStudies.summary: How a GenAI chatbot lifted conversion by 6%.

starr.situation: **Many customers dropped off** on the page showing our energy contracts. A contract is far harder to choose than an iPhone, so we assumed they had questions like "Which contract suits me best?"
starr.task: As Product Manager, I had to test whether **an AI sales chatbot** could answer them in the funnel, although customers might distrust AI.
starr.action: I had developers run a technical proof of concept. Then I **pitched the idea to the board** and brought in design, managers and a prompt engineer. We **reused the central platform's guardrails** and added our own, plus a ground truth. **In LangSmith, we reviewed every conversation.**
starr.result: Hallucinations dropped below 1% within two weeks. In the initial test, the funnel with the chatbot **converted 6% better**.
starr.reflection: After that, **a strong vision led us**. We shipped small customer-driven improvements without split tests, while tracking conversion, chat volume and prompts per chat as closely as we could.

caseStudies.title: Self-service agent Rens
caseStudies.summary: We let a Q&A agent handle requests too, cutting term amount tickets by 30%.

starr.situation: Rens, our n8n-built self-service bot, had already cut cost per contact by 13%. But **it only answered simple questions**, and its owner was stuck waiting for other teams' data.
starr.task: I pulled Rens into my team's portfolio to **make it act, not just answer**.
starr.action: I **moved it onto Coolblue's Virtual Agent Platform**, where website data was already connected. We started with the top request: changing the monthly term amount. Rens could only create tickets, and customer service had a 10-day backlog. Now it made the change itself. Changes of 30% or more went to a human, to avoid large final bills. **Legal approved the guardrails.**
starr.result: **Term amount tickets to customer service fell 30%**, and the backlog shrank from 10 to 9 business days.
starr.reflection: I first asked the wrong people how customer service handled these requests, and missed why guardrails mattered. Next time **I start with the team doing the work today**.

caseStudies.title: Regulatory pivot for 18 stores
caseStudies.summary: A new law forced a pivot in 18 stores, then stores outsold online.

starr.situation: From 2026, **new rules** required the welcome benefit for energy contracts in our 18 stores, a Coolblue discount, to become real money customers could spend anywhere.
starr.task: I had to make the benefit compliant without hurting store sales or forcing a big tech rebuild.
starr.action: Legal set hard limits, sales wanted no change, and tech needed a light solution. I mapped the risks and **pitched three scenarios to the board**. Paying everything at signing was risky, because customers could cancel after leaving. I recommended letting customers spend it in store immediately, with any unspent balance paid once supply started. **The board agreed.**
starr.result: We went live on 5 January 2026. **Store sales held to forecast** instead of dipping, and stores outsold online in the months after.
starr.reflection: I lost time winning support one stakeholder at a time. Now **I start with a decision document** and get the decision-makers into one room.

caseStudies.title: Greylisting against incentive fraud
caseStudies.summary: Greylisting logic cut potential fraud cases by 80%.

starr.situation: After our January 2026 store pivot, **incentive fraud dropped but did not stop**. People signed up in several stores under new names, emails and addresses, spent the discount of up to €300 in store and cancelled.
starr.task: The store sales manager spotted the problem. **I owned the technical fix.**
starr.action: With a process improver and the sales manager, I mapped the fraud cases. No single pattern stood out. An identity check came first, but it relied on store staff. So I **brought two development teams together on a greylisting logic**. Customers matching an existing contract or a recent cancellation could no longer spend the discount in store. They got it only once supply started.
starr.reflection: I learned to **roll out high-impact logic slowly**. Flagging honest customers would hurt our core proposition, so we went from one store to three, then nationwide.

caseStudies.title: Low-code in-store contract MVP
caseStudies.summary: A vibe-coded MVP helped stores pass €100,000 contract value monthly.

starr.situation: Stores sold energy contracts through our consumer website, and **staff handed out physical gift cards by hand**. It worked and had to scale.
starr.task: As owner of online sales from our stores, I had to **make contracting faster** for staff and customers.
starr.action: Automating gift cards in our React and Java stack would take too long, so **I chose a vibe-coded MVP** with our AI specialist. **Using Replit and n8n**, customers signed the legal terms and received a gift card code automatically. Leaving the application flow for an external page felt clunky, so once proven, **we moved terms and gift cards into the main flow**.
starr.result: Each sign-up got **about 30 seconds faster**. Alongside staff training, stores grew into our biggest sales channel, at over €100,000 in contract value a month.
starr.reflection: This changed my question. I stopped asking "what can my team build?" and started asking **"what resources can improve my product?"**

caseStudies.title: Heat pump mid-funnel recovery
caseStudies.summary: Unsure about a heat pump? A 72-hour prototype lifted conversion 3%.

starr.situation: Heat pump sales dropped. Our funnel only served customers who already wanted one: they left their details and sales called them. **Interested but unsure customers had nowhere to go.**
starr.task: I had to recover sales by serving this bigger mid-funnel group.
starr.action: Marketing spotted the gap, so I brought them together with my product team. Our designer's solution would cost two sprints, **too much for an untested hypothesis**. So I brought in our AI specialist, who **vibe-coded it in 72 hours**. Customers could check costs and heat pump types for their home and get a quote, which sales agents then followed up. After the test, **we rebuilt it properly in our funnel**.
starr.result: **Conversion rose 3%**, worth about €480k in extra sales a year.
starr.reflection: Vibe-coding is great for testing a hypothesis, but its tracking was unreliable, and tracking feeds every product decision. **I now weigh those flaws before I prototype.**

caseStudies.title: Funnel health
caseStudies.summary: Stores spotted outages first, until we proved over 99% uptime.

starr.situation: Store staff reported **website outages** in a Google Chat **before my team knew**. We were always reacting, and their trust in our sales flow suffered.
starr.task: I wanted us to **warn stores before they noticed**, and to prove our flow was reliable.
starr.action: My team lead built a Datadog dashboard tracking uptime of key pages across channels. I finalized it with him, focused on store opening hours. Datadog fit our website's structure, so it cost little sprint time. We then **shared the numbers with the stores**.
starr.result: The store application flow was **up over 99% of opening hours**. We now posted outage alerts in the store chat first, and stores replied with understanding.
starr.reflection: Store staff only try new features if they trust the flow. A website that breaks several times a day kills that. **Reliability is a precondition for adoption.**

caseStudies.title: Data-as-a-Product vision
caseStudies.summary: A data platform vision still guiding the team almost two years later.

starr.situation: Coolblue's central data platform team built what was new in the industry and shipped it **without asking the 15+ data teams it served**.
starr.task: As Data Product Owner, I had to **define who we built for and why**.
starr.action: I first talked with data team managers and analysts. Then I **ran vision sessions** with the domain manager, tech lead and senior engineers. Those interviews could bias me into steering the group, so **a neutral scrum master hosted**, briefed by me on what each session had to produce. The vision set out our product, its scope and its users.
starr.result: The team finally knew whom it served. Almost two years later, the Product Owner I coached confirmed **the vision still guided the team**.
starr.reflection: Vision work felt like too many hours at the time. Pushing through changed how the team behaved, from shipping without follow-up to **engineers talking with their stakeholders**.

caseStudies.title: Monte Carlo rollout
caseStudies.summary: A pilot team gained data visibility our internal tooling never gave.

starr.situation: Board members **could not always trust their report data**. My manager, the Head of Data, had started talks with Monte Carlo, a data observability tool.
starr.task: I had to take Monte Carlo from pilot to contract, then **get 15+ data teams to adopt it**.
starr.action: Instead of shipping it and expecting teams to follow, **I started with one**: the commercial team, which struggled most with reliability and liked new tools. Demos looked complete, but real pipelines exposed vague spots. I **let the team dig into those cases themselves**, which built confidence faster.
starr.result: The commercial team **saw more of its data streams** than our internal tooling ever showed. Other teams put commercial work first. I left just as reliability became measurable.
starr.reflection: We pushed adoption alone, without board backing. Next time I would get my manager to **make it a board priority first**, so teams made time.

caseStudies.title: Margin-aware cross-sell logic
caseStudies.summary: Two split tests lifted attached margin 7%, worth about €3.5M a year.

starr.situation: An automated logic picked which brand and model to show within each product type, weighing units sold against margin. **Nobody had revisited it.**
starr.task: As cross-sell Product Owner, I **owned attached margin per product** and had to grow it.
starr.action: With my analyst, I **ran a 28-day split test** rebalancing units against margin, then a second to push further. We **judged each test on total cross-sell profit**, not units or margin alone. After two wins, I built an engine so he could **tune the ratio himself, without developers**.
starr.result: **Attached margin per product rose 7%** (+4% and +3% against control), worth about €3.5M a year. The analyst ran a few more winning tests alone.
starr.reflection: I built the engine for one expert. When he left, no one could run it and the gains stalled. Now **I build for many users, not one**, and ship a cheaper shortcut first. That would have saved a sprint.

caseStudies.title: Cross-sell orchestration platform
caseStudies.summary: Why hardcode vendor deals when sales can do it? €140k in year one.

starr.situation: Our new cross-sell page ran on automated recommendations, but sales teams **sold spots on it to vendors** for €5k to €50k each.
starr.task: I had to honour those deals without losing the logic or my team's focus.
starr.action: At first we hardcoded vendor products by hand. **Each change took one developer hour** from the sprint goal. Once that lost time outweighed the cost of building a tool, I chose to **give sales the keys**. I shipped a platform where they overrode the logic themselves, and **the logic still filled every spot they left alone**.
starr.result: Over 100 sales and content colleagues used it. **Vendor placements added €140k** in the first 12 months, and hardcoded changes faded out as the platform matured.
starr.reflection: I tested with only a few users, then shipped to everyone, and adoption came slowly. Now I **grow a pilot group step by step**, with explanation and feedback before a full rollout.

caseStudies.title: Multi-market localization
caseStudies.summary: A reviews-first page for German shoppers lifted attached margin 8%.

starr.situation: Coolblue sold in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany, with Germany as the priority. **Cross-sell treated all three the same.**
starr.task: I had to make cross-sell fit each market **without splitting the platform**.
starr.action: One accessory could not be offered in Germany, so we either dropped it everywhere or invited German returns. I **added country-specific overrides** to the sales platform. German customers also lean on reviews far more than Dutch ones, so I **split-tested a German page that put reviews first**.
starr.result: **Attached margin per order in Germany rose 8%.** Sales could now run brand launches in one country only.
starr.reflection: My scope was cross-sell for the whole company, so I never studied Germany deeply. An adjacent team later found payment methods hurt German order completion. Today I would **start with cheap per-market tests** instead of assuming one design fits all.

caseStudies.title: Ambassador model
caseStudies.summary: Feedback from 100+ colleagues started arriving early enough to shape the build.

starr.situation: **Over 100 category team members** in sales, content and marketing relied on my products to grow attached margin. I owned cross-sell, upsell, installation services and our five website languages.
starr.task: I needed their **feedback early**, without losing my time for building.
starr.action: Feedback often reached me late or secondhand, which slowed development. A feedback form did not fix it, because it lacked personal contact. So I **divided the work with the existing specialists**, whom I spoke with daily. They handled what existing features or a Google Sheet could solve. **I met the teams myself** in presentations, one-on-ones and pilot groups.
starr.result: Category team members **started messaging me directly**, and feedback arrived while it could still shape the build.
starr.reflection: Balance was the hard part. Go too deep with every team and you lose the overview. Delegate everything and you build blind. I now **decide per topic** what I handle myself and what I delegate.
